name: Kerala

communities.name: Hindu
communities.notes: Kasavu mundu and set-mundu at festivals and temple visits; temples give flowers and sandal paste after worship.

communities.name: Muslim
communities.notes: Men: mundu (kara worn on the left by custom) with a shirt or long-sleeved kurta; embroidered Thalangara caps at festivals. Women traditionally: mundu with an embroidered kuppayam and a thattam head scarf; today churidar or saree with a headscarf, hijab or abaya. Largest in Malabar.

communities.name: Syrian Christian (Nasrani)
communities.notes: Older women's white chatta and mundu; married women wear the minnu pendant for life.

communities.name: Latin Christian
communities.notes: Many coastal fishing families in southern and central Kerala are Latin Catholic. Wedding and dress details still to research.

communities.name: Kurichiya (Wayanad)
communities.notes: Landowning farming community of Wayanad; matrilineal joint families; by custom apply sandal paste (kuri) on forehead and chest. Traditional dress not yet sourced.

communities.name: Kuruma (Wayanad)
communities.notes: Farming community of Wayanad; paddy cultivation central. Traditional dress not yet sourced.

excluded_communities.name: Cholanaikkan
excluded_communities.reason: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group of a few hundred people in the Nilambur forests with very limited outside contact until the 1960s; reusable characters would effectively depict a tiny, identifiable community.

look_range.hair: Mostly black, often thick and wavy or curly; long oiled hair in a single plait is common for older women.
look_range.notes: Wide range from wheatish to deep brown. Spread characters across the whole range. Starting range, tune after test renders.

adult_male.reason: The mundu is everyday and ceremonial wear across communities; kasavu marks festivals; Muslim men add a kurta and an embroidered cap at festivals.

adult_female.reason: Churidar is today's everyday wear (with a headscarf for many Muslim women); the kasavu set-mundu and the Mappila kuppayam with thattam are the signature festive dresses.

old_male.reason: Same as adult men; older men wear the mundu daily more often.

old_female.reason: Kasavu saree, chatta-mundu and kuppayam are the classic looks of older Hindu, Syrian Christian and Muslim women.

child_girl.reason: Churidar for school and everyday; pattu pavada for festivals.

child_boy.reason: Boys wear a small kasavu mundu at festivals.

avoid: Everyone in kasavu all the time: most daily life is churidar, shirts and trousers, lungi at home.
Elephants and houseboats in every image.
Thick moustache on every man as a shortcut for a Kerala man.
Mixing up Kerala and Tamil Nadu dress (Kanjeevaram silk is Tamil, not Kerala).
Skin tone pushed to one end of the range.
Showing Muslim women only in abaya: show the full range (kuppayam, churidar with headscarf, saree).
Treating Malabar as only Muslim or Travancore as only Hindu.
Caste labels, including for fishing communities; use occupation, never caste.
Kurichiya chieftain's ceremonial items on ordinary characters.
Theyyam or Kathakali costume on characters; these are ritual and performance forms, not dress.

naming.notes: Given name plus father's name or a house-name initial, e.g. 'Anjali Ramesh' or 'R. Anjali'. Do not use caste surnames (library rule).
Standard Arabic given names; father's name as second name is common.

seasons.monsoon: Southwest monsoon (Edavappathy) from June, northeast monsoon (Thulavarsham) from mid-October: umbrellas, wet streets, lush green.
seasons.summer: Between the monsoons the plains and coast stay warm and humid; hill stations stay cool all year. No real winter on the plains.

heritage.name: Theyyam
heritage.reason: A living form of worship in North Malabar: the performer is believed to become the deity, the costume is part of the deity's form, and the right to perform is hereditary within specific communities. Not costume, not decoration.

heritage.name: Historical Travancore and Kochi court dress
heritage.reason: Needs museum sources and the era system; fictional people only.

Corrected: Syrian Christian chatta and mundu limited to older women and to church, festive and ceremonial use (no longer daily wear), and the prompt now names the pleated fan (njori) at the back, as Wikipedia's Chattayum mundum page describes (use declined from the 1970s).

Checked: Balaramapuram and Kuthampully weaves are Kerala GI products; mundum neriyathum and the white gold-bordered saree confirmed by Wikipedia's Clothing in India; ela thali and the minnu with a cross confirmed by Wikipedia's Mangala sutra page.
